These teachings emphasize the unity of believers in Christ as one body with diverse members who should not harm one another.

3. In Luke 17:42-43: "Remember me, when you come into the kingdom of God" (μνήσθητί μου ὅταν ἔλθῃς ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ σου)

These statements indicate that Jesus describes the kingdom of God as something that doesn't come in a visible or observable way, is near, and believers should remember Jesus when they enter into this kingdom.

Based on the retrieved context, John teaches about abiding in Christ through two key passages:

1. In the Gospel of John (15:4-5), Jesus explains: "Abide in me, and I in you. The teaching emphasizes that abiding in Christ is essential for spiritual fruit production and is demonstrated by keeping Christ's commands. Without abiding in Christ, believers cannot bear fruit. Christ is the vine, and believers are the branches that must remain connected to Him to produce spiritual fruit.

Based on the retrieved context from 1 Corinthians, Paul teaches that believers form the body of Christ (σῶμα Χριστοῦ) with many members (μέλη). 

Specifically, Paul states in the context that:

1. Believers are "σῶμα Χριστοῦ" (the body of Christ) and "μέλη ἐκ μέρους" (members from parts) [27]

2. The body is one yet has many members: "Καθάπερ γὰρ τὸ σῶμα ἕν ἐστιν καὶ μέλη πολλ ὰ ἔχει, πάντα δὲ τὰ μέλη τοῦ σώματος πολλ ὰ ὄντα ἕν ἐστιν σῶμα" (the body is one and has many members, all members of the body that are many make one body) [12]

3. All believers are united in one body through baptism: "ἐν ἑνὶ πνεύματι ἡμεῖς πάντες εἰς ἓν σῶμα ἐβαπτίσθημεν" (we were baptized into one body in one Spirit) [13]

4. Members should care for one another: "ἵνα μὴ ᾖ σχίσμα ἐν τῷ σώματι, ἀλλ ὰ τὸ αὐτὸ ὑπὲρ ἀλλ ήλων μεριμνῶσι τὰ μέλη" (so that there may be no division in the body, but rather they should care for one another) [25]

5. The body functions as a unity: "εἴτε πάσχει ἓν μέλος, συμπάσχει πάντα τὰ μέλη" (if one member suffers, all members suffer together) [26]

Paul emphasizes that the body of Christ is one unified entity despite having many different members, and that members should work together in unity for the good of the whole body.

Based on the retrieved context from the SBLGNT (Society of Biblical Literature Greek New Testament) versions of John, here's what John teaches about light and darkness:

The Gospel of John states: "καὶ τὸ φῶς ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ φαίνει, καὶ ἡ σκοτία αὐτὸ οὐ κατέλαβεν" (And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it).

This teaching appears in multiple contexts in the Gospel of John:

1. The light (Christ) shines in the darkness of the world, but darkness cannot overcome the light.

2. John the Baptist came to testify about the light (Christ) so that people might believe through him: "οὗτος ἦλθεν εἰς μαρτυρίαν, ἵνα μαρτυρήσῃ περὶ τοῦ φωτός, ἵνα πάντες πιστεύσωσιν διʼ αὐτοῦ" (This came to testify about the light, so that they all may believe through him).

3. John himself was not the light, but came to testify about the light: "οὐκ ἦν ἐκεῖνος τὸ φῶς, ἀλλ ʼ ἵνα μαρτυρήσῃ περὶ τοῦ φωτός" (He was not the light, but that he might testify about the light).

4. The Gospel also teaches: "ὡς τὸ φῶς ἔχετε, ἵνα μὴ σκοτία ὑμᾶς καταλάβῃ" (As you have the light, so that darkness may not seize you).

5. Additionally: "ὡς τὸ φῶς ἔχετε, πιστεύετε εἰς τὸ φῶς, ἵνα υἱοὶ φωτὸς γένησθε" (As you have the light, believe in the light, so that you may become children of light).

In summary, John teaches that the light (Christ) shines in the darkness of the world, but darkness cannot overcome the light. Those who have the light (through faith in Christ) will not be seized by darkness and can become children of light.

The New Testament teaches that there are two fundamental commandments that constitute the entire law. In Matthew 22:38-40, Jesus states that "this is the great and first commandment" (αὕτη ἐστὶν ἡ μεγάλη καὶ πρώτη ἐντολή) - which is to love God with all one's heart, soul, and mind (εις κύριον τὸν θεόν σου ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ καρδίᾳ σου καὶ ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ ψυχῇ σου καὶ ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ διανοίᾳ σου).

The second commandment, described as "the second is like this" (Δευτέρα ὁμοία αὐτῇ), is to love your neighbor as yourself (Ἀγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον σου ὡς σεαυτόν).

The New Testament teaches that "the whole law is contained in these two commandments" (ἐν ταύταις ταῖς δυσὶν ἐντολαῖς ὅλος ὁ νόμος). This teaching appears consistently across the New Testament - in Mark 12:31, Jesus declares that loving your neighbor as yourself is "the greatest commandment" (μείζων τούτων ἄλλ η ἐντολὴ οὐκ ἔστιν).

The context shows that these two commandments (loving God and loving one's neighbor) are the essential foundation of the entire law, as summarized by Jesus in the New Testament.

Based on the retrieved context from 1 Corinthians, Paul teaches that believers form one body (the body of Christ) with many different members. Specifically:

1. The church is "one body" with "many members" (πολλ ὰ ἔχει) - "ἕν ἐστιν σῶμα, οὕτως καὶ ὁ Χριστός" (one body, just as Christ)

2. This body has unity despite diversity - "καὶ μέλη ἐκ μέρους" (and members from parts)

3. Members should care for one another - "ὑπὲρ ἀλλ ήλων μεριμνῶσι τὰ μέλη" (care for one another)

4. The body experiences unity in suffering and joy - "εἴτε πάσχει ἓν μέλος, συμπάσχει πάντα τὰ μέλη" (if one member suffers, all members suffer)

5. God has united the body together to prevent division - "ὁ θεὸς συνεκέρασεν τὸ σῶμα" (God has united the body)

6. The body is one but has many parts that function together - "πάντα δὲ τὰ μέλη τοῦ σώματος πολλ ὰ ὄντα" (all members of the body are many)

Paul emphasizes that believers are parts of one body (the church) that must care for one another, where the welfare of one member affects the whole body.

This teaching emphasizes that belief in Jesus (the light) leads to spiritual transformation and becoming children of light, while the context shows that this belief was not universally accepted despite Jesus' actions.

Based on the retrieved context from the Gospel of John (SBLGNT version), John teaches several important lessons about light and darkness:

1. "The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it" (John 1:5)

2. John the Baptist came to testify about the light (Jesus) so that all may believe through him, but he was not the light himself (John 1:35-36)

3. "Walk as you have the light, so that the darkness does not seize you, and the one walking in the darkness does not know where to go" (John 8:12)

4. "As you have the light, believe in the light, so that you may become children of light" (John 8:12)

John's teaching emphasizes that there is a distinction between those who walk in the light (those who believe in Jesus) and those who walk in darkness (those who do not believe). The light (Jesus) is the true source of enlightenment that reveals the way, while darkness represents spiritual blindness and separation from God. Those who follow the light will not be captured by darkness and will become children of light through faith in Jesus.

Based on the provided context from the New Testament, here's what the New Testament teaches about forgiveness:

The New Testament teaches that forgiveness is a reciprocal relationship that we are commanded to practice. Specifically:

1. We are instructed to forgive others "as we also have forgiven our debtors" (Matthew 6:12).

2. The text states that "if you forgive men's transgressions, your Father who is in heaven will also forgive you" (Matthew 6:14).

3. In Colossians, the New Testament teaches that Christians should "bear with one another and forgive one another, just as Christ forgave you" (Colossians 3:13).

4. The New Testament emphasizes that forgiveness is a necessary condition for receiving God's forgiveness - if we don't forgive others, God will not forgive us.

This teaching shows that forgiveness is both a command for believers and a key aspect of the Christian life, modeled by Jesus himself. The New Testament presents forgiveness as a reciprocal relationship where we forgive others as we have been forgiven by God.

Based on the retrieved context, John teaches that:

1. Eternal life is given by God (the Father) - "ζωὴν αἰώνιον ἔδωκεν ⸂ὁ θεὸς ἡμῖν⸃" (this is the eternal life that the Father has given us)

2. Eternal life exists in Jesus Christ (the Son) - "αὕτη ἡ ζωὴ ἐν τῷ υἱῷ αὐτοῦ ἐστιν" (this life is in His Son)

3. Those who have the Son have eternal life - "ὁ ἔχων τὸν υἱὸν ἔχει τὴν ζωήν" (he who has the Son has life)

4. Those who do not have the Son of God have no eternal life - "ὁ μὴ ἔχων τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ τὴν ζωὴν οὐκ ἔχει" (he who does not have the Son of God has no life)

5. Eternal life has been manifested (made visible) through Jesus Christ - "ἡ ζωὴ ἐφανερώθη" (the life became manifest)

This teaching appears in 1 John 1:1-3 where John describes how the eternal life that was with the Father has become visible to believers through Jesus Christ.

"37 Καὶ μὴ κρίνετε, καὶ οὐ μὴ κριθῆτε... ἀπολύετε, καὶ ἀπολυθήσεσθε"

The context also references the concept of "ἀφεῖναι" (to forgive or release from guilt) in the surrounding passages, but the specific teaching about forgiveness that Jesus provides in the context is clearly that we should forgive others to be forgiven by God.

Based on the retrieved context, Jesus teaches about prayer in the following ways:

1. He provides the model prayer (the Lord's Prayer) in Luke 11:1-4, which includes:
   - Addressing God: "Πάτερ, ἁγιασθήτω τὸ ὄνομά σου" (Father, hallowed be your name)
   - Seeking God's kingdom: "ἐλθέτω ἡ βασιλεία" (Let your kingdom come)
   - Requesting daily bread: "τὸν ἄρτον ἡμῶν τὸν ἐπιούσιον δίδου ἡμῖν τὸ καθʼ ἡμέραν" (Give us daily bread)
   - Asking for forgiveness: "καὶ ἄφες ἡμῖν τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν" (Forgive us our sins)

2. He instructs that prayer should be done privately, not in public for show. In Matthew 6:5-6, Jesus says: "καὶ ὅταν προσεύχησθε, οὐκ ἔσεσθε ὡς οἱ ὑποκριταί" (And when you pray, do not be like hypocrites) and "σὺ δὲ ὅταν προσεύχῃ, εἴσελθε εἰς τὸ ταμεῖόν σου καὶ κλείσας τὴν θύραν σου πρόσευξαι τῷ πατρί σου τῷ ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ" (But when you pray, go into your private room and close the door, and pray to your Father who is in secret).

Jesus emphasizes both the proper content of prayer (the Lord's Prayer) and the appropriate manner of prayer (private, not public for show).

Based on the retrieved context, Jesus teaches about humility in Luke 14:11 (as shown in the SBLGNT-Luke text):

"πᾶς ὁ ὑψῶν ἑαυτὸν ταπεινωθήσεται, ὁ δὲ ταπεινῶν ἑαυτὸν ὑψωθήσεται."

This translates to: "He who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted."

Jesus also emphasizes humility through the context of children: "Ἄφετε τὰ παιδία ἔρχεσθαι πρός με καὶ μὴ κωλύετε αὐτά, τῶν γὰρ τοιούτων ἐστὶν ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ" (Let the children come to me and do not hinder them, for the kingdom of God belongs to such as these).

Additionally, Jesus states: "ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, ὃς ἂν μὴ δέξηται τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ ὡς παιδίον, οὐ μὴ εἰσέλθῃ εἰς αὐτήν" (Verily I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a child will not enter it).

These teachings show that Jesus associates humility with the childlike quality that enables one to enter the kingdom of God, contrasting those who exalt themselves with those who humbly accept God's kingdom.

Based on the retrieved context, Jesus teaches that wealth and possessions present significant challenges for entering the kingdom of God. Specifically:

1. Jesus states that "if you want to be perfect, go and sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will receive treasure in heaven and follow me" (Matthew 6:20-21).

2. Jesus says that "it is difficult for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 19:23).

These teachings emphasize that material wealth can be an obstacle to spiritual discipleship, and true followers of Jesus must be willing to give up possessions to follow Him and enter God's kingdom. The context shows Jesus teaching that wealth requires significant sacrifice for those who wish to follow Him completely.

Based on the retrieved context, Paul teaches several important things about the law:

1. In Romans 2:20-3:12, Paul shows that those who boast in the law but break it defile God (ὃς ἐν νόμῳ καυχᾶσαι, διὰ τῆς παραβάσεως τοῦ νόμου τὸν θεὸν ἀτιμάζεις).

2. In Galatians 5:1-6, Paul teaches that believers should not return to law-based slavery: "στήκετε οὖν καὶ μὴ πάλιν ζυγῷ δουλείας ἐνέχεσθε" (stand therefore, and do not again enter into slavery).

3. Paul states that Christ has freed believers from the law: "τῇ ἐλευθερίᾳ ⸂ἡμᾶς Χριστὸς ἠλευθέρωσεν" (in freedom, Christ has freed us).

4. Paul emphasizes that those who try to be justified by the law are actually cutting themselves off from Christ: "ἐὰν περιτέμνησθε Χριστὸς ὑμᾶς οὐδὲν ὠφελήσει" (if you cut off from Christ, you will not profit).

5. Paul teaches that believers must not try to be justified by doing the whole law: "μαρτύρομαι δὲ πάλιν παντὶ ἀνθρώπῳ περιτεμνομένῳ ὅτι ὅλον τὸν νόμον ποιῆσαι" (I bear witness again that those who have been cut off must do the whole law).

The key message is that Paul teaches believers are freed from the law's slavery by Christ, and those who try to be justified by the law rather than by faith are actually breaking it and cutting themselves off from Christ.

Based on the retrieved context, Paul teaches that the resurrection of the dead is a crucial doctrine for Christian faith. In the context provided from Acts 17:32-33, Paul is speaking about hope and the resurrection of the dead (ἀναστάσεως νεκρῶν), identifying himself as a Pharisee who was teaching this doctrine.

The most detailed teaching about resurrection appears in the 1 Corinthians passage where Paul makes a logical argument: "If there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ did not rise from the dead" (1 Cor 15:13). He continues this argument by stating that if Christ didn't rise from the dead, then "the message of our faith is empty" (1 Cor 15:14). Paul emphasizes that Christ's resurrection is the foundation for the resurrection of believers, as he argues: "If Christ did not rise from the dead, then we have no hope" (1 Cor 15:17).

The context shows that Paul was addressing a debate between two groups - the Sadducees (who did not believe in resurrection) and the Pharisees (who did believe in resurrection) - and he was teaching that the resurrection of the dead is essential for Christian faith. His teaching demonstrates that the resurrection of Christ is necessary for the resurrection of believers and that without this doctrine, Christian faith has no meaning.

Based on the retrieved context, Paul teaches several important things about the Holy Spirit:

1. In Acts 65:6, Paul states that "when Paul laid hands on them, the holy Spirit came upon them" - showing that the Holy Spirit descends upon believers after baptism.

2. In 1 Corinthians 67:5, Paul teaches that "there are divisions of gifts, but the same Spirit" - indicating that the Holy Spirit is the source of various spiritual gifts that are distributed among believers.

3. In 1 Corinthians 67:6-7, Paul describes that "there are divisions of ministries, and the same Lord" and "there are divisions of powers, and the one who works all things in all" - showing the Holy Spirit's role in empowering believers for different ministries and powers.

4. In 1 Corinthians 67:8, Paul states that "to each person is given the manifestation of the spirit according to their need."

5. In 1 Corinthians 67:9, Paul explains that "for some, through the spirit, is given wisdom, for others, through the same spirit, is given knowledge" - demonstrating that the Holy Spirit distributes different spiritual gifts to different people.

These passages collectively show that Paul teaches about the Holy Spirit as the unifying power that comes upon believers, distributes various spiritual gifts to the church, and works all things in all aspects of Christian life.

Based on the retrieved context, Paul teaches several important characteristics of love in 1 Corinthians 13. According to the Greek text provided:

1. Love is greater than all other spiritual gifts and qualities - Paul states that love is greater than prophesy, knowledge, and faith (1 Corinthians 13:1-3).

2. Love is patient (μακροθυμεῖ) - it endures without becoming frustrated.

3. Love is kind (χρηστεύεται) - it is beneficial and constructive.

4. Love does not envy (οὐ ζηλοῖ)

5. Love does not boast (οὐ περπερεύεται)

6. Love does not act in a self-centered way (οὐ φυσιοῦται)

7. Love does not get easily angry (οὐκ ἀσχημονεῖ)

8. Love does not keep a grudge (οὐ ζητεῖ τὰ ἑαυτῆ)

9. Love never fails (οὐδέποτε πίπτει) - where prophetic gifts, tongues, and knowledge will cease (1 Corinthians 13:8-9)

Paul emphasizes that love is the most important quality among spiritual gifts, and that without love, even the greatest spiritual gifts become meaningless. This passage is one of the most famous teachings about love in the New Testament.

Based on the retrieved context from the New Testament, here's what the New Testament teaches about loving God and loving one's neighbor:

The New Testament teaches that:

1. Loving God involves the whole heart, whole soul, whole mind, and whole strength (Mark 62: "θεόν σου ἐξ ὅλης τῆς καρδίας σου καὶ ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς σου καὶ ἐξ ὅλης τῆς διανοίας σου καὶ ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ἰσχύος σου").

2. Loving your neighbor as yourself is presented as the greatest commandment (Mark 62: "Ἀγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον σου ὡς σεαυτόν" - "Love your neighbor as yourself").

3. This commandment (loving your neighbor as yourself) is more significant than all other commandments (Mark 62: "μείζων τούτων ἄλλ η ἐντολὴ οὐκ ἔστιν" - "This is the greatest commandment").

4. The New Testament teaches that the command to love your neighbor as yourself encompasses all other commandments (Romans 66: "Οὐ μοιχεύσεις, Οὐ φονεύσεις, Οὐ κλέψεις, Οὐκ ἐπιθυμήσεις, καὶ εἴ τις ἑτέρα ἐντολή, ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τούτῳ ἀνακεφαλαιοῦται" - "Do not commit adultery, do not kill, do not steal, do not covet, and if there is any other commandment, it is included in this").

5. The New Testament emphasizes that true love for God cannot exist without love for neighbor, and vice versa (1 John 83: "ὁ γὰρ μὴ ἀγαπῶν τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὐτοῦ ὃν ἑώρακεν, τὸν θεὸν ὃν οὐχ ἑώρακεν οὐ δύναται ἀγαπᾶν" - "Whoever does not love their brother whom they have seen cannot love God whom they have not seen").

6. The New Testament presents love for neighbor as the fulfillment of the law (Romans 66: "ὁ γὰρ ἀγαπῶν τὸν ἕτερον νόμον πεπλήρωκεν" - "Whoever loves their neighbor has fulfilled the law").

This teaching shows that in the New Testament, loving God and loving one's neighbor are deeply interconnected commands that form the foundation of Christian life, with love for neighbor being the greatest commandment that fulfills all other commandments.

Based on the retrieved context from the New Testament in Koine Greek (SBLGNT), the New Testament teaches the following about faith and works:

1. Faith without works is dead (James 2:17): "οὕτως καὶ ἡ πίστις, ἐὰν μὴ ἔχῃ ἔργα, νεκρά ἐστιν καθ' ἑαυτήν."

2. Justification comes through faith alone, not through works (James 2:24): "ὁρᾶτε ὅτι ἐξ ἔργων δικαιοῦται ἄνθρωπος καὶ οὐκ ἐκ πίστεως μόνον."

3. Abraham was justified by faith, not by works (James 2:21-22): "Ἀβραὰμ ὁ πατὴρ ἡμῶν οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων ἐδικαιώθη, ανενέγκας Ἰσαὰκ τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριον."

4. Faith works with works (James 2:22): "βλέπεις ὅτι ἡ πίστις συνήργει τοῖς ἔργοις αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐκ τῶν ἔργων ἡ πίστις ἐτελειώθη."

5. The Bible testifies that faith is counted as righteousness (Romans 4:11): "Ἐλογίσθη τῷ Ἀβραὰμ ἡ πίστις εἰς δικαιοσύνην."

The New Testament teaches that true faith is demonstrated by works, but justification (being made right with God) comes through faith alone. Faith without works is dead, while genuine faith produces good works as evidence of its authenticity.

This is specifically indicated in the passage from Acts 19:4 where Paul explains: "John baptized with a baptism of repentance, saying to the people that the one coming after me would be the one to believe" (πιστεύσωσιν).

This passage shows that Paul teaches that John's baptism was preparatory for faith in the coming one (Christ), emphasizing that faith comes through the coming of Christ rather than through John's baptism itself. Paul is making it clear that the purpose of John's baptism was to point toward the one who would be believed in (Christ).

The context does not provide additional specific teachings about faith beyond this passage, which is part of Paul's explanation to those who had been baptized in John's baptism.

Based on the retrieved context from the SBLGNT (Society of Biblical Literature Greek New Testament) versions of 1 John, John teaches that eternal life (ζωὴν αἰώνιον) is:

1. The life that was with the Father and became manifest (visible) - as stated in 1 John 1:2: "καὶ ἡ ζωὴ ἐφανερώθη, καὶ ἑωράκαμεν καὶ μαρτυροῦμεν καὶ ἀπαγγέλλομεν ὑμῖν τὴν ζωὴν τὴν αἰώνιον ἥτις ἦν πρὸς τὸν πατέρα καὶ ἐφανερώθη ἡμῖν" (and the life was made manifest, and we have seen and testify to you the life that is eternal which was with the Father and became manifest to us)

2. Received through having the Son of God - as stated in 1 John 1:12: "ὁ ἔχων τὸν υἱὸν ἔχει τὴν ζωὴν... ὁ μὴ ἔχων τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ τὴν ζωὴν οὐκ ἔχει" (He who has the Son has life... He who does not have the Son of God has no life)

John's teaching emphasizes that eternal life is not something that can be earned or attained through human effort, but is given through having the Son of God (Jesus Christ). Those who possess the Son of God receive eternal life, while those who do not have the Son of God lack eternal life.

Based on the retrieved context, Jesus teaches about wealth and possessions in these specific ways:

1. Jesus instructs someone to "sell all your possessions and give to the poor, and you will receive treasure in heaven, and come after me" (Mark 8:21).

2. Jesus states that "it is difficult for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God" (Luke 12:16-21).

3. He makes a comparison that "it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God" (Luke 12:21).

The context shows that Jesus emphasizes the challenge of wealth for entering God's kingdom, and provides the teaching that one should give up possessions to follow Him, though the person in the story goes away sorrowful because he had many possessions.

Based on the retrieved context, Jesus teaches about serving others in several key ways:

In Matthew 20:23-27 (as shown in the retrieved text), Jesus states: "οὐχ οὕτως ἐσται ἐν ὑμῖν ... ὃς ⸀ἂν θέλῃ ἐν ὑμῖν μέγας γενέσθαι ἔσται ὑμῶν διάκονος, 27 καὶ ὃς ⸀ἂν θέλῃ ἐν ὑμῖν εἶναι πρῶτος ⸀ἔσται ὑμῶν δοῦλος" (It will not be so in you... whoever wants to be great among you will be your servant, and whoever wants to be first among you will be your servant).

This teaching emphasizes that true greatness comes through service rather than through being first or having authority. Jesus teaches that those who want to be great in the community should become servants, and those who want to be first should be servants.

Additionally, in John, Jesus teaches that "ἵνα ἀγαπᾶτε ἀλλ ήλους, καθὼς ἠγάπησα ὑμᾶς" (that you may love your brothers, as I have loved you), showing that serving others is connected to loving others as Jesus loved us.

The retrieved context shows that Jesus' teaching on service is central to his message about how followers should relate to one another - through humility and service rather than power or authority.

Based on the retrieved context, Paul teaches in Galatians that Christians are not children of slavery but children of freedom (οὐκ ἐσμὲν παιδίσκης τέκνα ἀλλ ὰ τῆς ἐλευθέρας). 

Specifically, Paul states in Galatians 5:1-6 that:
- Christ has set us free (τῇ ἐλευθερίᾳ ⸂ἡμᾶς Χριστὸς ἠλευθέρωσεν)
- We should stand firm and not again be enslaved to the law (στήκετε οὖν⸃ καὶ μὴ πάλιν ζυγῷ δουλείας ἐνέχεσθε)
- If you are cut off from Christ (περιτέμνησθε Χριστὸς), you will gain nothing
- If you are separated from Christ (περιτεμνομένῳ), you must do the whole law (ὁ ὀφειλέτης ἐστὶν ὅλον τὸν νόμον ποιῆσαι)

Paul's teaching emphasizes that Christians are not under the law but are free from it through Christ, and that trying to be saved by the law (rather than by faith in Christ) leads to an impossible burden of doing the entire law.

Based on the retrieved context, John teaches about believing in Jesus through a specific passage from John 3:35-38 (as indicated by the numbering in the context). According to this passage:

Jesus asks the person: "Do you believe in the Son of Man?" (Σὺ πιστεύεις εἰς τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου)

The person responds by asking: "Who is the Son of Man? So that I may believe in Him."

Jesus then says: "And you have seen him who speaks with you; he is the one."

The person then declares: "I believe, Lord, and I worship you."

This passage shows that John teaches that genuine belief in Jesus requires:
1. Recognition of Jesus as the Son of Man (the title referring to Jesus himself)
2. More than just intellectual assent - true belief involves worship
3. The person must understand and accept who Jesus is (the Son of Man) before they can believe

The passage demonstrates that belief in Jesus results in worship, indicating that John's teaching emphasizes a personal, transformative relationship with Jesus rather than mere intellectual acknowledgment.

1. "The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it" (John 1:5)

These teachings show that light represents God's presence, truth, righteousness, and fellowship with God, while darkness represents sin, separation from God, and false teaching. John emphasizes the importance of walking in the light to maintain genuine fellowship with God and others.

Based on the retrieved context, John (Jesus) teaches about abiding in Christ in John 15:6-24. The key teaching appears in the passage where Jesus says:

"ἐὰν μείνητε ἐν ἐμοὶ καὶ τὰ ῥήματά μου ἐν ὑμῖν μείνῃ, ὃ ἐὰν θέλητε"

This translates to: "If you abide in me and my words abide in you, I will abide in you."

The context shows that this teaching is part of Jesus' larger teaching on the vine and branch metaphor (John 15). In this passage, Jesus explains that true abiding in Christ involves:

1. Remaining in Christ (abiding in Him)
2. Having Christ's words remain in the believer
3. This relationship results in Christ abiding in the believer

The context also shows that Jesus teaches about this relationship being essential for spiritual life and connection with God, as seen in the phrase "ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ⸂γνώσεσθε ὑμεῖς⸃ ὅτι ἐγὼ ἐν τῷ πατρί μου καὶ ὑμεῖς ἐν ἐμοὶ κἀγὼ ἐν ὑμῖν" (which means "in that day you will know that I am in my Father and you in me and I in you").

This teaching emphasizes the intimate, reciprocal relationship between Christ and the believer that enables spiritual life and growth.

GENERATED ANSWER
----------------------------------------------------------------------

Based on the retrieved context of New Testament passages in Koine Greek (Galatians and James), the New Testament teaches the following about faith and works:

1. Justification (being made right with God) comes not through works of the law but through faith alone. As shown in Galatians, "that one will not be justified by works of the law" (ὅτι ἐξ ἔργων νόμου οὐ δικαιωθήσεται).

2. True faith demonstrates itself through works, but faith without works is considered dead (ἀργή ἐστιν). James states: "faith without works is dead."

3. Abraham serves as an example: "Abraham was not justified by works" (Ἀβραὰμ ὁ πατὴρ ἡμῶν οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων ἐδικαιώθη).

4. The New Testament teaching emphasizes that genuine faith produces good works, but works are not the basis for justification. As James states: "if not having works, it is dead" (ἐὰν μὴ ⸂ἔχῃ ἔργα⸃, νεκρά ἐστιν).

The New Testament presents a balanced view where faith is the foundation of salvation, but true faith necessarily produces works that demonstrate its authenticity. Works are not the means of justification but the evidence of genuine faith that has been transformed by the Spirit of God.

The New Testament teaches that resurrection is not merely a future event but has present significance through the believer's union with Christ in his death and resurrection, with the promise of a future resurrection that occurs before the final judgment.

Based on the retrieved context, the New Testament teaches about forgiveness through the process described in Matthew 18:15-18 (as shown in the text):

1. When someone sins against you, you should first go to that person privately to ask for forgiveness (ἀπολύετε, καὶ ἀπολυθήσεσθε - "go to them and ask for forgiveness")

2. If they don't listen to you, you can involve others by bringing one or two witnesses with you (παράλαβε μετὰ σοῦ ἔτι ἕνα ἢ δύο - "take one or two more with you")

3. If they still don't listen, you can treat them as an outsider (εἰπὸν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ - "treat them as an outsider")

The context also indicates that Jesus has the authority to forgive sins (ἐξουσίαν ἔχει ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἀφιέναι ἁμαρτίας - "Jesus has authority to forgive sins").

This teaching emphasizes the process of handling forgiveness when someone has sinned against you, showing that forgiveness is a process that involves approaching the person first, seeking reconciliation, and if necessary, involving others while still maintaining the possibility of reconciliation.

In Matthew 5:44 (as referenced in the context), Jesus says: "But I say to you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you."

Jesus' teaching on loving enemies is part of his broader instruction that believers should "do good without expecting anything in return" (as mentioned in Luke 6:36). This teaching represents a radical command that contrasts with conventional expectations of society, calling believers to respond to hostility with love and blessing rather than retaliation.

Based on the retrieved context, Jesus teaches about forgiveness in several important ways:

1. In Matthew 6:20-23, Jesus explains that he has the authority to forgive sins (ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἔχει ἐξουσίαν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἀφιέναι ἁμαρτίας), and he uses this authority to forgive people's sins (Ἄνθρωπε, ἀφέωνταί σοι αἱ ἁμαρτίαι σου).

2. In Luke 6:36-38, Jesus teaches that we should be merciful as our Father is merciful (γίνεσθε οἰκτίρμονες καθὼς ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν οἰκτίρμων ἐστίν). He emphasizes that forgiveness and mercy flow naturally from a life of non-judgment (καὶ μὴ κρίνετε, καὶ οὐ μὴ κριθῆτε) and releasing others (ἀπολύετε, καὶ ἀπολυθήσεσθε).

3. Jesus connects forgiveness with the principle of giving (δίδοτε, καὶ δοθήσεται ὑμῖν), teaching that when we forgive others, we receive from God - "a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and stored up, will be given to you."

The context shows that Jesus teaches forgiveness as both a divine authority (to forgive sins) and a practical ethic of life (being merciful, not judging, releasing others).

In Matthew 4:1-4, Jesus states: "Τίς ἄρα μείζων ἐστὶν ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῶν οὐρανῶν;" (Who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?) and explains that "ἐὰν μὴ στραφῆτε καὶ γένησθε ὡς τὰ παιδία, οὐ μὴ εἰσέλθητε εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν" (Unless you become like children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven).

Jesus teaches that true greatness comes through humility - becoming like children (who are humble) is necessary to enter the kingdom of heaven, and whoever humbles himself as a child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven.

1. "the kingdom of God is within you" (v.21: ἰδοὺ γὰρ ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ἐντὸς ὑμῶν ἐστιν)

2. "the kingdom of God is near" (v.31: ἐγγ ύς ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ)

3. The kingdom of God is like children (v.16: τῶν γὰρ τοιούτων ἐστὶν ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ)

4. "Whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a child will not enter it" (v.17: ὃς ἂν μὴ δέξηται τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ ὡς παιδίον, οὐ μὴ εἰσέλθῃ εἰς αὐτήν)

Jesus emphasizes that the kingdom of God is present within people and requires a childlike humility to enter, rather than being something that can be achieved through human effort or status.

In this context, Jesus emphasizes that repentance is not merely an emotional state but should be demonstrated through tangible actions that produce fruit worthy of the change in heart.

1. We are the body of Christ ("We are the body of Christ and members" - 1 Corinthians 12:27)

2. The body consists of many members ("For the body is not one member but many" - 1 Corinthians 12:14)

3. Each member has a specific role that God has set in the body ("But God has set each member in the body as He willed" - 1 Corinthians 12:18)

5. The body functions properly only through diversity - "If all were one member, where would the body be?" (1 Corinthians 12:19)

6. The body is one unified whole despite having many parts - "Now we have many members, but one body" (1 Corinthians 12:20)

Paul emphasizes that the church is the body of Christ with diverse members that work together in unity, each serving a specific purpose within the whole.

Based on the retrieved context from the Gospel of John (SBLGNT), here's what John teaches about light and darkness:

1. The light has come into the world (John 1:4-5), and "the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it."

2. People loved darkness more than light because "their works were evil" (John 3:9).

3. Those who do evil "hate the light and do not come to the light, that his works may not be exposed" (John 3:20).

4. In contrast, "the one who does the truth comes to the light, that his works may be made manifest that they are done in God" (John 3:21).

5. John teaches that people should "believe in the light, that you may become sons of light" (John 3:36).

The core teaching is that light represents truth, righteousness, and relationship with God, while darkness represents sin and separation from God. The Gospel of John emphasizes that those who are in darkness (sinful) reject the light, while those who follow truth come into the light to reveal their righteous works done in God.

1. Christ's resurrection is a central doctrine that is repeatedly mentioned and emphasized throughout the New Testament texts provided. The context shows references to "περὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως τοῦ χριστοῦ" (about the resurrection of Christ) in Acts.

2. The New Testament teaches that if Christ did not rise from the dead, then Christian faith would be futile. As seen in 1 Corinthians, there is a clear statement that "εἰ δὲ Χριστὸς οὐκ ἐγήγερται, ματαία ἡ πίστις" (if Christ was not raised, faith is futile).

4. The New Testament teaches about the resurrection of believers, as indicated by statements like "εἰ δὲ νεκροὶ οὐκ ἐγείρονται" (if dead men are not raised).

The context shows that the resurrection of Christ is a foundational teaching for Christian faith, with significant implications for the nature of Christian belief and the hope of believers.

Based on the retrieved context, the New Testament teaches the following about forgiveness:

1. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus addresses the concept of forgiveness of sins, with a teaching that questions whether it's better to say "your sins are forgiven" or "rise and walk" (Matthew 9:1-2).

2. The Gospel of Luke emphasizes practical forgiveness in relationships: "If your brother sins against you, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him. And if he sins against you seven times a day and repents seven times, you must forgive him" (Luke 17:3-4).

3. The Epistle to Colossians teaches that Christians should "bear with one another and forgive one another, just as Christ forgave you, so you should do" (Colossians 3:12-13), with love being "the bond of perfection."

The New Testament teaches that forgiveness is both a divine gift (forgiveness of sins) and a practical command for believers to forgive others repeatedly, with the emphasis on loving relationships and the importance of reconciliation when others repent.

Based on the retrieved context from the Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Jesus Christ feels that the Pharisees do not know who he is (the Christ). 

In John 1:26-27, Jesus states: "κἀμὲ οἴδατε καὶ οἴδατε πόθεν εἰμί" (I am the one you seek) and "καὶ ἀπʼ ἐμαυτοῦ οὐκ ἐλήλυθα, ἀλλʼ ἔστιν ἀληθινὸς ὁ πέμψας με, ὃν ὑμεῖς οὐκ οἴδατε" (I did not come from myself, but the one who sent me is true). This shows that Jesus is aware the Pharisees do not recognize who he is.

Additionally, in John 1:23, there is a reference to "ὁ κόσμος ὀπίσω αὐτοῦ ἀπῆλθεν" (the world has gone away from him), indicating a sense of separation between Jesus and the Pharisees.

The context shows Jesus' perspective that the Pharisees lack understanding of his identity and purpose, which creates a spiritual distance between them. This is consistent with the broader New Testament understanding that Jesus' mission was to those who would recognize him as the Messiah, not those who were disconnected from his message.

Based on the retrieved context, Jesus teaches that we should forgive others in order to receive forgiveness from God. Specifically, in Luke 6:37-38 (as shown in the context), Jesus says:

"καὶ ἀπολύετε, καὶ ἀπολυθήσεσθε" (Forgive, and you will be forgiven)

The context also shows that Jesus teaches we should not judge or condemn others, as this leads to being judged or condemned by God: "καὶ μὴ κρίνετε, καὶ οὐ μὴ κριθῆτε" (Do not judge, and you will not be judged) and "καὶ μὴ καταδικάζετε, καὶ οὐ μὴ καταδικασθῆτε" (Do not condemn, and you will not be condemned).

Based on the retrieved context from the SBLGNT (Standard Greek New Testament), Jesus teaches about humility in Luke 14:14. The specific teaching is:

"ὁ δὲ ταπεινῶν ἑαυτὸν ὑψωθήσεται, ὁ δὲ ἑαυτὸν ὑψωθήσεται."

This translates to: "The humble will be exalted, and the exalted will be humbled."

This teaching emphasizes that humility (the state of humbling oneself) leads to exaltation, while pride (the state of exalting oneself) leads to humiliation. This is a fundamental teaching about humility in Jesus' ministry.

The context also shows that Jesus associates humility with children (in Luke 14:16), saying "Let the children come to me and do not prevent them, for the kingdom of God belongs to such as these," suggesting that humility is a characteristic of those who enter God's kingdom.

Based on the retrieved context, Jesus speaks about the kingdom of God in Luke 18-23, where he uses two parables to explain what the kingdom of God is like:

1. In verse 19: "ὁμοία ἐστὶν κόκκῳ σινάπεως, ὃν λαβὼν ἄνθρωπος ἔβαλεν εἰς κῆπον ἑαυτοῦ, καὶ ηὔξησεν καὶ ἐγένετο εἰς δένδρον, καὶ τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ κατεσκήνωσεν ἐν τοῖς κλάδοις αὐτοῦ." (It is like a mustard seed which a man takes and puts in his field, and it grows and becomes a tree, and the birds of the heavens make their nests in its branches.)

2. In verse 21: "ὁμοία ἐστὶν ζύμῃ, ἣν λαβοῦσα γυνή ἔκρυψεν εἰς ἀλεύρου σάτα τρία ἕως οὗ ἐζυμώθη ὅλον." (It is like yeast which a woman takes and hides in three measures of flour until it is leavened throughout.)

Jesus also states in verse 43 of the passage: "καὶ ταῖς ἑτέραις πόλεσιν εὐαγγ ελίσασθαί με δεῖ τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ, ὅτι ἐπὶ τοῦτο ἀπεστάλην." (And it is necessary for me to preach the kingdom of God, for this I was sent.)

These passages show that Jesus taught that the kingdom of God is a powerful, growing force that begins small but eventually becomes large and provides shelter for many (the mustard seed parable), and it is also transformative like yeast that works throughout a larger system (the yeast parable).

Based on the retrieved context, Jesus teaches several important lessons about wealth and possessions:

1. Jesus instructs followers to sell their possessions and give to the poor in order to receive treasure in heaven and follow him (Matthew 21:21, Luke 18:22).

2. Jesus states that it is "difficult for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 23:23, Luke 18:24).

3. Jesus compares how difficult it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God - "How difficult it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God" (Luke 18:24).

4. In a more dramatic illustration, Jesus says that "it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God" (Luke 18:25).

The context shows that Jesus presents wealth as a significant obstacle to entering the kingdom of God, and encourages giving up possessions to follow him, while emphasizing that this is a difficult path for those who are wealthy.

Based on the retrieved context, Jesus teaches about repentance using the significant metaphor of a tree that produces good fruit. Specifically:

1. Jesus instructs his listeners to "ποιήσατε οὖν καρπὸν ἄξιον τῆς μετανοίας" (make fruit worthy of repentance) - meaning true repentance involves producing tangible, good fruit in one's life.

2. He emphasizes that "πᾶν οὖν δένδρον μὴ ποιοῦν καρπὸν καλὸν ἐκκόπτεται καὶ εἰς πῦρ βάλλ εται" (any tree that does not produce good fruit is cut down and burned) - this illustrates that without genuine repentance (producing good fruit), people will face judgment.

3. Jesus warns against claiming Abraham as their father in the spiritual sense, saying "μὴ δόξητε λέγειν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς Πατέρα ἔχομεν τὸν Ἀβραάμ" (do not say in yourselves "We have Abraham as Father") - indicating that true repentance requires a new identity beyond the old ways.

4. He explains that "δύναται ὁ θεὸς ἐκ τῶν λίθων τούτων ἐγεῖραι τέκνα τῷ Ἀβραάμ" (God can raise children to Abraham from these stones) - showing that God's grace can transform people who truly repent.

Jesus' teaching on repentance therefore emphasizes that it's not merely an emotional state but a practical response that produces good fruit in one's life, with consequences for those who do not demonstrate this change.

1. In John 64:34, Jesus says: "I give you a new commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you" (Greek: ἐντολὴν καινὴν δίδωμι ὑμῖν ἵνα ἀγαπᾶτε ἀλλ ήλους, καθὼς ἠγάπησα ὑμᾶς ἵνα καὶ ὑμεῖς ἀγαπᾶτε ἀλλ ήλους)

3. Jesus emphasizes giving to the poor: In John 64:30, Jesus takes bread and gives it to the poor, and in Mark 62:21, He says: "Sell what you have and give to the poor"

4. Jesus teaches a principle of reciprocity: "Give, and it will be given to you" (Luke 63:38)

5. Jesus also teaches about being merciful: "Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful" (Luke 63:36)

These teachings show that Jesus emphasizes loving others, especially the poor and enemies, giving without expectation, and serving through mercy and selfless action.

Based on the retrieved context, Paul teaches about grace in Galatians 3:3 where he states: "χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη ἀπὸ θεοῦ πατρὸς ⸂καὶ κυρίου ἡμῶν⸃ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ" (Grace and peace to you from God our Father, and from our Lord Jesus Christ).

1. A gift from God the Father
2. A gift from Jesus Christ (our Lord)
3. Given to believers as a fundamental aspect of the Christian relationship

The context also shows that Paul teaches grace is the foundation for believers' calling (Galatians 6:6), and that believers should not turn away from this grace to follow another gospel. Paul specifically states in Galatians 6:6: "Θαυμάζω ὅτι οὕτως ταχέως μετατίθεσθε ἀπὸ τοῦ καλέσαντος ὑμᾶς ἐν χάριτι Χριστοῦ εἰς ἕτερον εὐαγγ έλιον" (I marvel that you have so quickly turned away from the calling you received in the grace of Christ to another gospel).

This shows Paul's teaching that grace is the essential gift that believers receive through Christ, which forms the basis of their relationship with God and should not be abandoned for other teachings.

Based on the retrieved context from 1 Corinthians and Ephesians, Paul teaches several important things about the body of Christ:

1. The church is one unified body (σῶμα) with many parts (μέλη), though it is one single entity: "For just as the body is one and has many parts, all the parts are one body, so also is Christ."

2. All believers are baptized into one body: "For we were all baptized into one body, into one Spirit, whether Jews or Greeks, slaves or free."

3. The body consists of many different members that each have a specific role: "For the body is not one member, but many members." Paul uses examples like eyes, ears, feet to show how different parts serve different functions.

4. God deliberately arranged the members for the common good: "But God has set the members of the body, one member to another, as He willed."

5. The body requires unity and mutual care: "If one member suffers, all members share in that suffering." Paul emphasizes that members should not cause division but work together for the common good.

6. Christ is the head of the body: "For Christ is the head, and all the body is joined together in him."

7. The body needs to be built up through service: "For the purpose of the holy ones to work in service, to build up the body of Christ."

Paul's teaching centers on the unity, diversity of roles, and interdependence within the church as the body of Christ, with Christ as its head.

John identifies this presence of the Holy Spirit as what makes Jesus "the elect of God" (ὁ ⸀ἐκλεκτὸς τοῦ θεοῦ). This teaching emphasizes the visible descent of the Holy Spirit and His abiding presence on Jesus as the one who is baptized in the holy Spirit.

Based on the retrieved context from the Gospel of John and 1 John, John teaches the following about light and darkness:

1. In the Gospel of John (1:4-5), John teaches that "the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it" (καὶ τὸ φῶς ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ φαίνει, καὶ ἡ σκοτία αὐτὸ οὐ κατέλαβεν). This indicates that truth (light) exists and remains active even in the world of sin (darkness).

2. In 1 John (1:5), John teaches that "God is light and darkness is not in him" (ὁ θεὸς φῶς ἐστιν καὶ σκοτία ⸂ἐν αὐτῷ οὐκ ἔστιν⸃ οὐδεμία). This emphasizes that God is pure, without sin or darkness.

John's teaching shows that light represents truth, life, and God's presence, while darkness represents sin, falsehood, and separation from God. The light persists and does not get overcome by darkness, indicating that truth remains active even in a world that is not fully aligned with it.

Based on the retrieved context, the New Testament teaches that loving God and loving one's neighbor are fundamental commands with specific emphasis:

In Mark 12:28-31, Jesus explicitly teaches that the first commandment is to love God with all one's being: "Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God is one Lord." The second commandment is to love one's neighbor as oneself. Jesus states that "there is no commandment greater than these."

The context also shows that in 1 John, there is a direct connection between loving God and loving one's neighbor: "If anyone says, 'I love God,' and hates his brother, he is a liar, for he who does not love his brother whom he has seen, cannot love God whom he has not seen."

Additionally, Romans 13:8-10 indicates that "Love your neighbor as yourself" is the fulfillment of the law, showing that this commandment encompasses all other commandments.

The New Testament presents these two aspects of love as interconnected, with the command to love God with all one's heart, soul, strength, and mind being the foundation, and the command to love one's neighbor as oneself being the practical application that fulfills the law.

# What the New Testament Teaches About Faith and Works

Based on the retrieved New Testament passages, the New Testament teaches that **faith alone justifies a person before God, while works are not the basis for justification but rather evidence of genuine faith**.

## Key Teachings:

1. **Faith is the foundation of justification**: 
   - The New Testament consistently shows that Abraham was justified by faith ("Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness" - Romans 4:3, Galatians 3:6)
   - Faith is what makes a person righteous before God, not human works

2. **Works do not justify**:
   - "A man is justified by works and not by faith alone" (James 2:24) - This is a clear teaching that works cannot be the basis for justification
   - "For it is written that whoever does not abide by all the commandments in the book of the law will be under wrath" (Galatians 5:10) - This shows that the law (which requires works) does not save

3. **Faith produces works**:
   - "You see that faith works with his works and through his works faith was perfected" (James 2:22) - Genuine faith produces good works as evidence of true saving faith
   - "Those who are by faith are blessed with Abraham" (Galatians 3:9) - Faith produces the blessings of Abraham's covenant

4. **The distinction between justification and works**:
   - "The wage of the worker is not counted by grace but by obligation" (Romans 4:4) - Works are not the means of justification but the result of justified faith
   - "The law is not by faith, but he who does the works will live by them" (Romans 4:13) - This shows that the law's purpose is to guide those who are already justified, not to justify

The New Testament teaching is that true faith produces good works as evidence of its authenticity, but these works are not the basis for salvation or justification. Salvation comes through faith in Christ, not through human efforts or works.

This teaching is clearly summarized in James 2:14-26, where the New Testament emphasizes that faith without works is dead, while genuine faith produces works that are evidence of that faith.

Based on the retrieved context from the SBLGNT (Society of Biblical Literature Greek New Testament), I can provide the following information about resurrection teachings in the New Testament:

The New Testament teaches that:

1. Christ's resurrection is foundational - "Christ has been raised from the dead" (1 Corinthians 15:20) and this event confirms that "Christ has been raised from the dead, and does not die again" (Romans 6:9).

2. Believers are united with Christ in His death and will be raised with Him - "For since we were made partakers of the likeness of His death, we also shall be raised to the resurrection of the dead" (Romans 6:8).

3. Jesus declares Himself to be "the resurrection and the life" (John 11:25), meaning that through Him, believers have hope of resurrection.

4. There is a specific order of resurrection - "just as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive" (1 Corinthians 15:22) and "each person will be raised in their own order" (1 Corinthians 15:23).

5. The resurrection of believers is connected to the death of Adam - "as all died through Adam, so all will be made alive through Christ" (1 Corinthians 15:22).

6. Believers who die with Christ will be raised with Him - "If we die with Christ, we also will live with Him" (Romans 6:8).

7. The resurrection is not merely physical but involves a transformation of life - believers are "dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus" (Romans 6:11).

The New Testament teaches that resurrection is a central promise for believers, with Christ's resurrection being the foundation for this hope and the beginning of the process that will ultimately result in all believers being raised to eternal life.

Based on the retrieved context, the New Testament teaches about forgiveness in these specific ways:

1. In Luke 6:37-38, there's a direct teaching about forgiveness: "καὶ μὴ κρίνετε, καὶ οὐ μὴ κριθῆτε" (And do not judge, and do not be judged), "καὶ μὴ καταδικάζετε, καὶ οὐ μὴ καταδικασθῆτε" (And do not condemn, and do not be condemned), "ἀπολύετε, καὶ ἀπολυθήσεσθε" (And release, and be released), and "δίδοτε, καὶ δοθήσεται ὑμῖν μέτρον καλὸν πεπιεσμένον" (Give, and it will be given to you a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and flowing over).

2. The context also references a parable in Matthew (likely Matthew 18:23-35) about forgiveness where a servant who was forgiven a huge debt by his master later refuses to forgive a fellow servant who owed him a smaller amount.

The New Testament teaching emphasizes that forgiveness is reciprocal - when we forgive others, God will forgive us and we will receive "a good measure" of blessings that exceeds what we give. The context shows that forgiveness is a necessary component of the Christian life, with consequences for those who fail to forgive others.

Based on the retrieved context, Jesus teaches about loving one's enemies in Luke 6:27-28 (as shown in the SBLGNT Greek text). Specifically, Jesus says:

"ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑμῶν, καλῶς ποιεῖτε τοῖς μισοῦσιν ὑμᾶς, εὐλογεῖτε τοὺς καταρωμένους, προσεύχεσθε περὶ τῶν ἐπηρεαζόντων ὑμᾶς."

This translates to: "Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, and pray for those who treat you ill."

This teaching appears in the context as part of Jesus' Sermon on the Mount where he challenges his followers to go beyond normal social expectations by demonstrating active love and compassion toward those who are hostile or adversarial toward them.

Based on the retrieved context, Paul teaches that faith is:

1. A response to the Holy Spirit - As seen in Acts 19:2 where Paul says "Εἰ πνεῦμα ἅγιον ἐλάβετε πιστεύσαντες" (If you receive the holy spirit, believe)

2. Involves belief in Christ - Paul explains that John baptized "βάπτισμα μετανοίας" (a baptism of repentance) saying "εἰς τὸν ἐρχόμενον μετʼ αὐτὸν ἵνα πιστεύσωσιν, τοῦτʼ ἔστιν εἰς τὸν Ἰησοῦν" (to the one who would come to be baptized to believe, that is to Christ)

3. Connected with repentance - The context shows that faith is part of a process that includes repentance (as indicated by John's baptism of repentance)

4. The basis for salvation - The context indicates that faith in Christ is what leads to salvation, as seen in the Colossians passage where it mentions "ἀκούσαντες τὴν πίστιν ὑμῶν ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ" (hearing your faith in Christ Jesus)

Paul's teaching emphasizes that faith is a response to the Holy Spirit and involves belief in Christ as the one who brings salvation through the process of repentance.

Based on the retrieved context, John teaches that eternal life is received through faith in Jesus. Specifically, in John 6:47, it states: "ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, ὁ πιστεύων ἔχει ζωὴν αἰώνιον" (I tell you truly, whoever believes has eternal life).

Additionally, in 1 John 5:13, John writes: "Ταῦτα ἔγραψα ⸀ὑμῖν ἵνα εἰδῆτε ὅτι ζωὴν ⸂ἔχετε αἰώνιον⸃ , ⸂τοῖς πιστεύουσιν⸃ εἰς τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ" (I wrote this to you so that you may know that you have eternal life, to those who believe in the name of the Son of God).

John's teaching connects eternal life with faith in Jesus as the Son of God and emphasizes that this eternal life is a gift received through belief. The context also shows that eternal life is connected to having fellowship with God (John 1:3, 1 John 5:13).

Based on the retrieved context from the Septuagint Greek Bible (SBLGNT), Jesus teaches several important principles about forgiveness:

1. In Luke 6:37-38, Jesus explicitly states: "Do not judge, and do not be judged... forgive, and you will be forgiven." This is a direct teaching about the reciprocal nature of forgiveness - if we forgive others, God will forgive us.

2. In Mark 62:25, Jesus teaches: "And when you stand praying, forgive whatever you have against anyone, so that also your Father who is in heaven will forgive you your debts." This shows that forgiveness is an active practice we should engage in during prayer, with the promise that God will forgive us when we do so.

3. Jesus also teaches about the connection between forgiveness and receiving forgiveness: "Give, and it will be given to you in a good measure, and you will be filled." This reflects the idea that when we forgive others, we open ourselves to receiving forgiveness and grace from God.

The most comprehensive teaching about forgiveness in this context is that forgiveness is a reciprocal relationship - when we forgive others, we create space for God's forgiveness to flow into our lives. Jesus emphasizes that forgiveness is not something we do for the sake of rules or external conditions, but rather a fundamental aspect of how we relate to God and others.

This teaching aligns with the broader Christian understanding that forgiveness is both a gift from God and an active practice that transforms our relationships with others.

"οὐχ οὕτως δέ ⸀ἐστιν ἐν ὑμῖν<tool_call> ἀλλ ʼ ὃς ⸀ἂν θέλῃ ⸂μέγας γενέσθαι⸃ ἐν ὑμῖν, ἔσται ὑμῶν διάκονος, 44 καὶ ὃς ⸀ἂν θέλῃ ⸂ἐν ὑμῖν εἶναι⸃ πρῶτος, ἔσται πάντων δοῦλος"

This means: "But it is not so with you. Whoever wants to be great among you, let him be your servant, and whoever wants to be first among you, let him be your slave."

Jesus teaches that those who seek to be great (μέγας) should become servants (διάκονος), and those who seek to be first (πρῶτος) should become servants (δοῦλος). This is a direct teaching about humility - that true greatness comes through humility and service to others, not through self-centered power or position.

The context also indicates that Jesus teaches humility through the contrast between worldly attitudes (those who want to rule over others) and the humble attitude he promotes, where true leadership comes through service and humility.

2. "Verily I say to you that whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a child will not enter it" (verse 17) - This emphasizes that the kingdom of God requires a childlike attitude and humility.

3. "Thus you also, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near" (verse 31) - This indicates that the kingdom of God is imminent and will come when certain signs occur.

4. The kingdom of God "does not come with observation" (verse 21) - This suggests that the kingdom of God is not something that can be observed or seen in the conventional sense.

5. Jesus uses the lightning analogy to describe the suddenness of the kingdom of God: "For just as the lightning that comes from heaven and lights up the heaven, so will be the Son of Man in his day" (verse 24) - This illustrates that the kingdom of God will come suddenly and unexpectedly.

These statements collectively show that Jesus describes the kingdom of God as something that is near, accessible to humble people, comes suddenly, and requires a childlike attitude to enter.

Based on the retrieved Koine Greek context, Jesus teaches that wealth and possessions present significant challenges for entering the kingdom of God. Specifically:

1. In Mark 10:21, Jesus instructs someone to "sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven, and follow me."

2. In Luke 18:22-25, Jesus states that it is "how difficult it is for those who have riches to enter the kingdom of God." He uses a powerful metaphor comparing it to "how easier it is for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God."

3. The context shows that Jesus emphasizes a radical change of heart regarding possessions - the person who is wealthy becomes "sorrowful" when hearing this teaching because he "was very rich."

4. Jesus' teaching indicates that true wealth is not in material possessions but in spiritual treasure - "you will have treasure in heaven" rather than earthly wealth.

The key message is that while possessions are not inherently wrong, Jesus teaches that those who have wealth must make significant sacrifices to follow him and enter the kingdom of God, as material wealth creates a barrier to spiritual transformation.

Based on the retrieved context from the SBLGNT (Standard Biblical Greek New Testament), Jesus teaches about repentance in the following ways:

1. Jesus instructs his followers to "produce fruit worthy of repentance" (ποιήσατε οὖν καρπὸν ἄξιον τῆς μετανοίας in Matthew 3:8 and ποιήσατε οὖν καρποὺς ἀξίους τῆς μετανοίας in Luke 3:8).

3. Jesus explains that true repentance involves understanding that God can raise children from stones to Abraham (δύναται ὁ θεὸς ἐκ τῶν λίθων τούτων ἐγεῖραι τέκνα τῷ Ἀβραάμ).

4. This teaching is given in the context of baptism, where Jesus is saying that people should produce this kind of fruit as a response to the call for repentance.

The context shows that Jesus connects repentance with producing meaningful spiritual fruit rather than just claiming Abraham as their spiritual ancestor, indicating that true repentance involves a transformation of life rather than superficial claims.

Based on the retrieved context, Paul teaches about justification in Romans 18-21 as follows:

Paul explains that justification (δικαίωσιν) comes through one righteousness (δικαιώματος) rather than through sin. As stated in the text: "Therefore, just as by one sin we all come to judgment, so also by one righteousness we all come to justification of life."

The context shows that Paul teaches that justification is achieved through the obedience (ὑπακοή) of one person. This is clearly stated in Romans 19: "Just as many sinners were made righteous by the obedience of one person, so also many will be made righteous by the obedience of one righteousness."

Paul's teaching contrasts the consequences of sin (which leads to judgment) with the consequences of righteousness (which leads to justification of life). This teaching emphasizes that justification is not based on human works but through the obedience of Christ, who is the one person through whom justification occurs.

The context indicates that Paul's teaching about justification is part of his broader argument about how righteousness (δικαιώματος) relates to the Law and the Gospel, with the concept of justification being presented as a gift that leads to life rather than condemnation.

# What Paul Teaches About Grace

Based on the retrieved Koine Greek texts from Galatians and Ephesians, Paul teaches several important aspects of grace:

1. **Grace as the foundation of Christian life**: In both letters, Paul begins with "χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη" (grace and peace) from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, showing that grace is fundamental to Paul's teaching.

2. **Grace as the means of deliverance**: In Galatians 4, Paul states that Jesus gave himself "ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν" (for our sins) so that we might be delivered from the "αἰῶνος τοῦ ἐνεστῶτος" (the present age of evil) according to God's will.

3. **The gospel of grace**: In Galatians 6, Paul is amazed that believers have "μετατίθεσθε ἀπὸ τοῦ καλέσαντος ὑμᾶς ἐν χάριτι Χριστοῦ εἰς ἕτερον εὐαγγέλιον" (turned away from the gospel of grace that called them to another gospel), indicating that Paul teaches that the gospel is specifically about grace.

4. **Grace as the means of reconciliation**: In Ephesians, Paul describes how through grace believers have been "ἐν Χριστῷ" (in Christ) - brought near to God through the gift of Christ.

5. **Grace as a gift that sets believers apart**: Paul emphasizes that grace is the distinguishing factor that separates believers from the world and from the "αἰῶνος τοῦ ἐνεστῶτος" (the present age of evil).

Paul's teaching consistently shows that grace is not something believers earn through works, but a gift from God that delivers believers from sin and evil, establishes their relationship with God, and sets them apart as holy and blameless in Christ.

Based on the retrieved context, Paul teaches that the law has both importance and limitations. 

In Acts 15, Paul acknowledges the law as something that needs to be understood when addressing the Jews: "εἰ δὲ ζητήματά ἐστιν περὶ λόγου καὶ ὀνομάτων καὶ νόμου τοῦ καθʼ ὑμᾶς, ὄψεσθε αὐτοί" (But if there are questions about law, names, and the law that you have, look to them).

In Romans 2, Paul teaches that boasting in the law (νόμῳ καυχᾶσαι) is actually dishonoring God through breaking the law: "ὃς ἐν νόμῳ καυχᾶσαι, διὰ τῆς παραβάσεως τοῦ νόμου τὸν θεὸν ἀτιμάζεις" (Who boasts in the law, through breaking the law, dishonors God).

The context also shows that Paul teaches that the law has been fulfilled in Christ, as he speaks about Jesus "ἀπό τε τοῦ νόμου Μωϋσέως καὶ τῶν προφητῶν ἀπὸ πρωῒ ἕως ἑσπέρας" (from the law of Moses and the prophets).

Paul's teaching about the law emphasizes that it shows what is right and wrong but cannot save people. The law has a role in revealing sin, but it has been fulfilled through Christ.

Based on the retrieved context, Paul teaches several key points about the resurrection:

1. The resurrection of Christ is foundational to Christian faith - if Christ did not rise from the dead, then "the faith of yours is useless, and you remain in your sins."

2. There will be a universal resurrection of the dead - "just as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive."

3. The resurrection occurs in a specific order:
   - First, Christ rises from the dead ("the beginning of those who sleep")
   - Then, those who are with Christ will be raised
   - Finally, "the end" when "the kingdom is given to God and father"

4. The resurrection is a guarantee of eternal life - "if we are alive in Christ, we are more precious than all people"

5. Paul emphasizes that the resurrection of Christ is the basis for the resurrection of believers - "if Christ did not rise, then there is no resurrection of the dead"

Paul argues that the resurrection of Christ is essential to the Christian message, stating that if Christ didn't rise from the dead, then "the message of ours is empty and your faith is empty." He testifies that they were "witnesses to God that Christ was raised, who did not rise if the dead do not rise."

Based on the retrieved context from Paul's writings, I can identify several key teachings about the Holy Spirit:

1. The Holy Spirit is described as "holy" (ἁγίου) - This appears in the phrase "ἡγιασμένη ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ" (sanctified in the holy spirit) in Romans 16.

2. The Holy Spirit possesses power (δυνάμει) - In Romans 15:19, Paul states: "ἐν δυνάμει σημείων καὶ τεράτων, ἐν δυνάμει πνεύματος..." (in power of signs and wonders, in power of the Spirit).

3. The Holy Spirit is involved in the sanctification of believers - The context shows that believers are "sanctified in the holy spirit" (ἡγιασμένη ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ), indicating the Holy Spirit's role in the process of spiritual purification.

4. The Holy Spirit empowers believers to teach others - Paul states that believers are "full of knowledge" (πάσης γνώσεως) and "able to teach others" (ἀλλ ήλους νουθετεῖν), which suggests the Holy Spirit provides the gift of teaching.

These teachings appear in Paul's letters, particularly in the Romans passage where he emphasizes the holy nature of the Spirit and the Spirit's role in empowering believers for ministry. The context shows that Paul consistently presents the Holy Spirit as both the divine agent of sanctification and the source of spiritual empowerment for believers.

GENERATED ANSWER

Based on the retrieved context, Paul teaches several important things about the body of Christ:

1. The body of Christ is one unified body consisting of many different members (parts), as stated in 1 Corinthians 12:13: "For we were all baptized into one Spirit, and we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, slaves or free."

2. The body is not a single part but many members working together: "For the body is not one member, but many members" (1 Corinthians 12:14).

3. Each member has a specific function and purpose within the body, as demonstrated by Paul's examples of different body parts (eyes, feet, etc.) that all serve necessary functions.

4. Paul emphasizes that God has designed the body so that "the weaker members receive more honor" and "the less beautiful among us have more honor" (1 Corinthians 12:22-23).

5. The body is designed by God to function as a unified whole: "For God has united the body, giving more honor to the weaker" (1 Corinthians 12:25).

6. The body of Christ functions with unity and care for each other: "So that there is no division in the body, but each member cares for the others" (1 Corinthians 12:26).

7. In Ephesians, Paul teaches that "the head of the body is Christ" (Ephesians 1:15), and that the body is "built up in service" for the purpose of becoming "one unity in the faith and knowledge of the Son of God" (Ephesians 1:13).

8. The body of Christ is to be built up "in love" with each member contributing to the overall unity of the body (Ephesians 1:16).

This teaching emphasizes the importance of unity, diversity of functions, mutual care, and the divine design of the body of Christ as a single entity with Christ as its head.

Based on the retrieved context, Paul teaches that salvation comes through faith in Jesus Christ. The specific passage from Acts 16:31 shows this clearly: "Πίστευσον ἐπὶ τὸν κύριον Ἰησοῦν, καὶ σωθήσῃ σὺ καὶ ὁ οἶκός σου" (Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you and your house will be saved).

In Galatians, Paul further explains that salvation comes through Christ's sacrifice: "τοῦ δόντος ἑαυτὸν ὅπως ἐξέληται ἡμᾶς ἐκ τοῦ αἰῶνος τοῦ ἐνεστῶτος πονηροῦ" (the one who gave himself so that we might be delivered from the age of evil).

According to the context, Paul's teaching on salvation emphasizes faith in Jesus Christ as the means of salvation, with the understanding that this salvation delivers believers from the age of evil according to God's will.

Based on the provided Koine Greek context from the Gospel of John (64-SBLGNT-John.txt), John teaches about believing in Jesus in the following ways:

1. Belief in Jesus is blessed even when one does not see Him - John states: "μακάριοι οἱ μὴ ἰδόντες καὶ πιστεύσαντες" (blessed are those who do not see and yet believe).

2. Belief leads to having life in Jesus' name - John writes: "πιστεύοντες ζωὴν ἔχητε ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι" (that you may have life in His name).

3. True belief involves a personal relationship with Jesus - In John's teaching, Jesus instructs: "μὴ γίνου ἄπιστος ἀλλ ὰ πιστός" (do not become an unbeliever but a believer).

These passages show that John emphasizes that belief in Jesus is not merely intellectual but involves a personal relationship that brings spiritual life, and that this kind of faith is blessed even for those who have not seen Jesus physically.

Based on the retrieved context, John teaches about light and darkness in the following ways:

In John 1:4-5 (from the 64-SBLGNT-John.txt passage), John teaches that "In him was life, and the life was the light of men." He also states that "the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it."

In 1 John 1:5-6 (from the 83-SBLGNT-1John.txt passage), John teaches that "the light of the world is in you" and that if believers have fellowship with God and walk in the light, the darkness (sin) does not overcome them.

John's teaching emphasizes that true light represents fellowship with God and the presence of Christ (the "light of the world"), while darkness represents separation from God and sin. The light shines in the darkness but the darkness does not overcome it, indicating that God's light is ultimately victorious over darkness.

This teaching appears in both the Gospel of John and the First Epistle of John, showing consistent themes about light and darkness in John's writings.

# What John Teaches About Abiding in Christ

Based on the provided Greek text (SBLGNT) passages from John and 1 John, here's what John teaches about abiding in Christ:

## In John 15 (the primary teaching):
- **Abiding in Christ produces fruit**: "If you abide in me and my words are in you, I will abide in you, and whatever you ask in my name, it will be done" (John 15:7)
- **Abiding in Christ is connected to love**: "As the Father loved me, so I have loved you; abide in my love" (John 15:9)
- **Abiding in Christ involves keeping Christ's commands**: "If you keep my commands, you abide in my love, as I have kept the commands of my Father and I abide with him in love" (John 15:10)
- **Abiding in Christ leads to becoming Christ's disciples**: "This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you" (John 15:12)

## In 1 John 2:
- **Abiding in Christ provides boldness**: "And now, children, abide in him, so that if he appears, we may have boldness and not be ashamed before him in his presence" (1 John 2:28)
- **Abiding in Christ results in being born of Christ**: "If you know that he is righteous, you know that whoever does righteousness is born of him" (1 John 2:29)

John teaches that abiding in Christ is a vital relationship where believers:
1. Keep Christ's commands
2. Experience His love
3. Receive abundant spiritual fruit
4. Have boldness before Christ
5. Be "born of Him" spiritually

This abiding relationship is not merely a passive state but an active, ongoing process that enables believers to live in Christ's love and power.

Based on the retrieved context, the New Testament teaches that there are two commandments that are the greatest in the law:

1. The first commandment is to love God with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength (as seen in Mark 12:30 and Matthew 22:37-38)

2. The second commandment is to love your neighbor as yourself (as seen in Matthew 22:38)

The context specifically shows that Jesus identifies these two commandments as the greatest in the law. In the SBLGNT text, Matthew 22:37-38 states: "37 δὲδὲ WH Treg NIV ⸀τῇ⸀τῇ Treg NIV ⸁τῇ⸁τῇ WH Treg NIV ⸀τῇ⸀τῇ RP 38 ἡ μεγάλη καὶ πρώτηἡ μεγάλη καὶ πρώτη WH Treg NIV"

The context also indicates that these two commandments are interconnected, as shown in 1 John 5:1-2 where it states that those who love God also love others: "Πᾶς ὁ πιστεύων ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἐστιν ὁ χριστὸς ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ γεγέννηται, καὶ πᾶς ὁ ἀγαπῶν τὸν γεννήσαντα ἀγαπᾷ ⸀καὶ τὸν γεγεννημένον ἐξ αὐτοῦ" (Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and who loves the one who sent him, also loves the one who was sent).

The New Testament presents these two commandments as foundational to Christian life, with love for God and love for neighbor being intrinsically connected.

Based solely on the retrieved context from the Greek New Testament (SBLGNT) of James, I can provide this answer:

The New Testament (specifically James) teaches that faith without works is dead. The text states: "For just as the body without spirit is dead, so also faith without works is dead" (verse 26).

The passage emphasizes that Abraham, our father, was justified not by works but by faith (verses 21-22). James contrasts two perspectives: "You see that a person is justified by works and not only by faith" (verse 24), while also teaching that "the faith which is without works is dead."

The context shows that true faith produces works - "you see that faith works with his works and through works faith is perfected" (verse 22). James argues that justification comes through faith, not by works, and that faith without observable works is not genuine.

Based on the retrieved context, the New Testament teaches the following about resurrection:

1. Christ's resurrection is foundational to Christian belief - as shown in 1 Corinthians 15:13-22 where it states "Christ has been raised from the dead, the beginning of those who sleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20).

2. The resurrection of believers is connected to Christ's resurrection - "If Christ has not been raised, then your faith is futile" (1 Corinthians 15:17).

3. Believers will be resurrected from the dead in a specific order - "For Christ has been raised from the dead, the beginning of those who sleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20), followed by "Each in their own order" (1 Corinthians 15:23).

4. The resurrection transforms believers from death to life - "As in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive" (1 Corinthians 15:22).

5. The resurrected believers will have a transformed body - "Jesus, who is made alive from the dead in you, the one who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will make alive your mortal bodies through the Spirit that dwells in you" (Romans 8:11).

6. The resurrected believers will be like angels in heaven - "When they rise from the dead, they do not marry, but are as angels in heaven" (Mark 12:24).

The New Testament teaches that resurrection is not a future event for all at once, but occurs in a specific sequence beginning with Christ, followed by believers who will be transformed from mortal to immortal bodies.

The context shows that Jesus "knows" the Pharisees (John 20:17: "I know you"). In the Matthew passage, Jesus questions the Pharisees about who the Christ is, revealing their spiritual limitations in understanding (Matthew 22:41-46). 

Jesus also shows compassion for the spiritual condition of the Pharisees, as seen in Mark 2:17 where he states: "It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick" - indicating he sees the Pharisees as needing spiritual healing rather than being in a position of spiritual health.

The context doesn't explicitly state Jesus' feelings in emotional terms, but shows his relationship with the Pharisees through his knowledge of them, his teaching to them, and his recognition of their spiritual limitations.

Based on the provided Greek text context, Jesus teaches about loving one's enemies in Matthew 5:44 (as indicated by the verse numbering in the text). 

The specific teaching is found in verse 44: "ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν, ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ⸀ὑμῶν καὶ προσεύχεσθε ὑπὲρ ⸀τῶν διωκόντων ὑμᾶς"

This translates to: "But I say to you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you."

This teaching is part of Jesus' Sermon on the Mount, where He is instructing His followers on how to live ethically and lovingly. In this passage, Jesus goes beyond the common understanding of the time (which would have been to "love your neighbor" or "hate your enemies") and specifically commands His followers to love those who oppose them and to pray for those who persecute them.

This teaching represents one of Jesus' most profound ethical teachings about love and forgiveness, emphasizing that true love extends to those who are hostile toward us.

Based on the retrieved context, John teaches that eternal life (αἰώνιος ζωή) is:

1. The knowledge of the only true God and Jesus Christ (John 3:3): "αὕτη δέ ἐστιν ἡ αἰώνιος ζωὴ ἵνα γινώσκωσι σὲ τὸν μόνον ἀληθινὸν θεὸν καὶ ὃν ἀπέστειλας Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν."

2. Given to those who believe in the name of the Son of God (1 John 5:13): "Ταῦτα ἔγραψα ⸀ὑμῖν ἵνα εἰδῆτε ὅτι ζωὴν ⸂ἔχετε αἰώνιον⸃ , ⸂τοῖς πιστεύουσιν⸃ εἰς τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ."

3. Connected with having the Son (1 John 5:12): "ὁ ἔχων τὸν υἱὸν ἔχει τὴν ζωήν"

4. The life that was made visible (John 1:4): "καὶ ἡ ζωὴ ἐφανερώθη"

John presents eternal life as something that people receive through faith in Jesus Christ, which enables them to know God and is characterized by the relationship with the Son of God.
